title: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
summary: How eBPF runs verified programs at kernel and user hooks, and how bpftrace turns one-liners into them: probe types, the verifier's rules, in-kernel maps and histograms, and the cost model for production.
outcomes: Explain how a bpftrace one-liner becomes verified, JIT-compiled eBPF attached to a kernel hook
Choose between tracepoints, kprobes, fentry/fexit, uprobes and profile for stability, context and cost
Predict whether the verifier accepts a program: null checks, initialized registers, bounded loops, 1M limit
Compute hist() power-of-2 buckets and time calls with the @start[tid] pattern
Estimate tracing overhead as event rate x cost per event and pick map aggregation over printf

lessons.title: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel

blocks.md:
Suppose a production database box has sudden latency spikes and you suspect slow file reads. You want to know **which process** is reading, **how long each read takes**, and **how the latencies are distributed**, right now, without restarting anything.

Recall from the perf lesson that `perf record` samples or records events into a buffer, and the analysis happens later in user space. That works well for CPU profiles, but a question like "time every `read` per process and give me a histogram" needs custom logic that runs at the moment each event happens.

The obvious tools all have a catch:

- **strace** uses ptrace and stops the traced process on system calls so a separate tracer process can inspect them. Its own man page warns that a traced process runs more slowly.
- **Adding printk to the kernel** means patching, rebuilding and rebooting, which is exactly what you cannot do on the box that is misbehaving.
- **A custom kernel module** can run code at any point, but one bug (a bad pointer, an endless loop) crashes or hangs the whole machine.

What you want is the module's power with a guarantee that your code cannot break the kernel.

**eBPF** provides that. An eBPF program is a small program, written as bytecode for a simple virtual instruction set, that the kernel runs when an event (a *hook*) fires: a system call, a kernel function entry, a tracepoint, a timer. Before it is attached, the kernel's **verifier** proves the program is safe: it terminates, never reads an uninitialized register and never touches memory out of bounds. A **JIT** compiler then translates the bytecode into native machine code, so it runs at near native speed.

Programs keep state in **maps**: kernel data structures (hash tables, arrays, per-CPU variants, ring buffers) that both the eBPF program and user space can read and write. The name once stood for Berkeley Packet Filter; today eBPF is treated as a standalone name.

**bpftrace** is a high-level tracing language on top of eBPF, inspired by awk, C, DTrace and SystemTap. You write a probe, an optional filter and an action, and bpftrace compiles it with LLVM into eBPF bytecode and loads it through libbpf:

- `probe /filter/ { action }`
- `@name[key]` is a **map**; functions like `count()` and `hist()` say how the map is filled.
- When bpftrace exits (for example on Ctrl-C) it prints every map by default.

blocks.code:
# count system calls per process name, print on Ctrl-C
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:raw_syscalls:sys_enter { @[comm] = count(); }'

# trace file opens as they happen
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat { printf("%s %s\n", comm, str(args.filename)); }'
blocks.caption: Two one-liners from the official bpftrace tutorial. comm is the current process name; args holds the tracepoint's arguments.

blocks.title: From a one-liner to code running inside the kernel

scenes.caption: In user space, bpftrace parses your script and uses LLVM to emit eBPF bytecode. Nothing has touched the kernel yet.
The bytecode is handed to the kernel with the bpf() system call. The verifier walks every possible path through the program before anything runs.
If any path could loop forever, read uninitialized memory or go out of bounds, the load is refused and you get the verifier's log. The kernel is never at risk.
A program that passes is JIT-compiled to the CPU's instruction set and attached to its hook. From now on it runs every time the event fires.
Each run updates maps inside the kernel. When you press Ctrl-C, bpftrace reads the maps through the bpf() system call and prints them.

blocks.title: 1,000 reads: printf per event versus a count() map

scenes.caption: With printf, every event is copied out to user space and bpftrace formats a line for it. The formatting happens in user space, per event.
The other 999 reads each send their own record. At high event rates this per-event traffic is what makes tracing expensive, and records can be dropped if user space falls behind.
With @[comm] = count(), the same 1,000 events only increment a counter inside the kernel. Nothing crosses to user space per event.
At exit, bpftrace reads the finished summary once. 1,000 events became one small map read: this is why bpftrace prefers aggregating in maps.

blocks.md: eBPF lets you run your own logic at the moment an event happens, inside the kernel, with a load-time proof that it cannot crash or hang the machine. bpftrace makes that a one-liner: probe, optional filter, action, and maps that summarize in the kernel.

The verifier is a **safety** check, not a security review. It proves your program cannot crash or hang the kernel; it does not judge what the program observes. That is why loading tracing programs requires root, or both the CAP_BPF and CAP_PERFMON capabilities.

blocks.question: Why is a kernel module a poor way to add ad hoc tracing to a production machine, compared with an eBPF program?
options: A module cannot read kernel function arguments
Nothing checks the module's code before it runs, so one bad pointer or endless loop can crash or hang the whole machine
Modules can only be loaded at boot time
Modules run in user space and are therefore slow
blocks.explain: Modules run arbitrary native code in the kernel with no load-time safety proof. eBPF programs are verified first (termination, initialized registers, in-bounds memory) and only then JIT-compiled and attached.

blocks.question: You need per-process counts of 2 million syscalls per second. Which bpftrace action is cheapest?
options: printf the process name on every event and count lines with sort and uniq -c
Write each event to a file with system()
They cost the same, since all run in the kernel
@[comm] = count(), printed once at exit
blocks.explain: count() updates a map inside the kernel, so nothing crosses to user space per event. printf sends a record per event that user space must read and format, which is far more work at millions of events per second.

lessons.title: Probes: kprobes, tracepoints, fentry, uprobes and profile

blocks.md:
A **probe** is a named instrumentation point. In bpftrace it is written `provider:options`, for example `kprobe:vfs_read` or `tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat`. `bpftrace -l 'pattern'` lists probes and accepts `*` and `?` wildcards; `bpftrace -lv` also shows each probe's arguments.

Probe types differ on two axes: **where** they attach (kernel or user code, a function or a fixed marker, or a timer) and **how stable** they are across software versions.

scenes.caption: Kernel dynamic tracing: a kprobe can attach to almost any kernel function at runtime. Powerful, but the function names and arguments are internal details that change between kernel versions.

fentry and fexit also attach to kernel functions, through a BPF trampoline (a generated stub that calls your program) and BTF (the kernel's built-in type info), so args are typed, and fexit still sees them on return.
Kernel static tracing: tracepoints are hooks compiled into the kernel source by its developers. They are the preferred choice because their interface is meant to stay stable.
The same split exists in user space: uprobes attach to any function in a binary or library, while usdt probes are static markers the developers built in.
Finally, profile fires on every CPU at a fixed rate (sampling, like perf), and interval fires on one CPU for periodic output or timeouts.

blocks.md:
**How a kprobe works.** When a kprobe is registered, the kernel copies the probed instruction and overwrites its first byte(s) with a breakpoint instruction (`int3` on x86). When a CPU reaches it, it traps; the kprobes code runs the attached handler (here, your eBPF program), single-steps the saved copy of the original instruction, then resumes after the probe point.

On x86 kernels built with `CONFIG_OPTPROBES`, many kprobes are later **optimized**: the breakpoint is replaced with a jump, which avoids the trap and lowers the cost per hit. Also, a kprobe on a function's first instruction (like `kprobe:vfs_read`) is usually ftrace-based on x86: it uses the function's ftrace call site, with no breakpoint. The breakpoint path below is the general mechanism.

blocks.title: One hit on kprobe:vfs_read, then kretprobe on return

scenes.caption: At attach time, kprobes saves a copy of vfs_read's first instruction and writes a breakpoint over it. The running kernel is patched in memory, with no reboot.
A thread calls vfs_read. The CPU executes the breakpoint and traps, saving the registers, which is where arg0, arg1 and so on come from.
kprobes runs the attached eBPF program with the saved registers as its context. Your filter and action execute here, on the same CPU, in the thread's context.
kprobes single-steps its copy of the original instruction and resumes vfs_read. Stepping a copy avoids removing the breakpoint, so other CPUs never slip past it.
A kretprobe swaps the return address at entry for a trampoline. When vfs_read returns, the trampoline fires the return handler (retval is available), then jumps to the real caller.

blocks.md:
**Arguments and context.** For `kprobe`, and `uprobe` without debug info, you read raw arguments as `arg0`, `arg1`, ... taken from CPU registers (each an int64 you may need to cast). For `tracepoint`, `rawtracepoint`, `fentry` and `fexit`, arguments come as a typed `args` struct. `retval` holds the return value in `kretprobe`, `uretprobe` and `fexit`. Useful builtins: `pid`, `tid`, `comm` (process name), `nsecs` (nanosecond timestamp), `kstack` and `ustack` (stack traces).

The builtins describe **whichever thread is on the CPU when the probe fires**, which is not always the thread you care about.

Probe context matters. `tracepoint:block:block_rq_issue` often fires in the context of the process that issued the I/O, but it can also fire from kernel context (for example readahead), so `comm` and `pid` may not name the application you expect.

blocks.code:
# stable: syscall tracepoint, typed args
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_exit_read /pid == 18644/ { @bytes = hist(args.ret); }'

# dynamic: any kernel function, raw return value
bpftrace -e 'kretprobe:vfs_read { @bytes = lhist(retval, 0, 2000, 200); }'

# sampling: kernel stacks at 99 Hz on every CPU (flame graph input)
bpftrace -e 'profile:hz:99 { @[kstack] = count(); }'
blocks.caption: Adapted from the bpftrace one-liner tutorial. /pid == 18644/ is a filter: the action runs only when it is true.

blocks.question: You are writing a script that teammates will run for years across kernel upgrades. It counts file opens per process. Which probe should you choose first?
options: kprobe:do_sys_openat2, because kprobes can reach any function
uprobe on libc's open wrapper
tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat, because tracepoints are stable interfaces in the kernel source
profile:hz:99, because sampling has the lowest overhead
blocks.explain: Tracepoints are placed by kernel developers and meant to keep a stable interface. Internal function names that kprobes target can be renamed or change arguments between versions. A libc uprobe misses programs that make the syscall directly, and sampling would miss most opens.

blocks.question: In a kretprobe on a function, you try to print arg0 to see which file descriptor was passed in. What goes wrong, and what fixes it?
options: Arguments are not available at return in a kretprobe; save them in a map keyed by tid at entry, or use fexit, which still has args
Nothing; arg0 is preserved for kretprobe
kretprobes cannot access any data at all; use printf instead
You must cast arg0 to a pointer first
blocks.explain: A kretprobe only has retval: argument registers may have been overwritten by the time the function returns. Save what you need at entry, keyed by tid, or use fexit, whose args remain available on return.

lessons.title: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs

blocks.md:
The verifier is what makes it acceptable to run your code inside a production kernel. To understand its rules, picture the machine it checks. eBPF has **11 registers**, `r0` to `r10`, all 64 bits wide. `r1` to `r5` pass arguments to helper calls, `r0` holds return values, `r6` to `r9` are preserved across calls, and `r10` is a **read-only frame pointer** to a stack of at most **512 bytes**. At program start, `r1` points to the *context* (for a kprobe, the saved registers).

Programs cannot call arbitrary kernel functions. They call **helpers**, a fixed API the kernel exposes per program type, such as map lookup, reading the time or reading memory safely.

The verifier works in two steps. First it builds the control flow graph and rejects unreachable code and malformed jumps. Then it **simulates every path** from the first instruction, tracking for each register and stack slot a *type* (uninitialized, scalar, pointer to context, pointer to map value, pointer to map value *or NULL*, pointer to stack) and, for scalars, a range of possible values. Each branch forks the state, and both sides are explored.

The trace below is a simplified, hand-written program of the kind a map update compiles to: look up a map slot, then atomically increment it. Watch the register types.

blocks.title: The verifier tracking register types, path by path
blocks.code:
r1 = map[@counts]            ; pointer to the map
r2 = r10                     ; r10 = read-only frame ptr
r2 += -8                     ; r2 = address of key slot
*(u64 *)(r10 - 8) = 0        ; write the key (0)
call bpf_map_lookup_elem     ; r0 = value ptr or NULL
if r0 == 0 goto L1           ; null check
r1 = 1
lock *(u64 *)(r0 + 0) += r1  ; atomic add into value
L1: r0 = 0
exit

scenes.caption: Start: r1 is the context pointer, r10 the frame pointer, everything else is unreadable. Line 1 loads a map pointer into r1 (the context pointer is dropped).
r2 becomes a pointer into the stack at offset -8. Any access through it must stay inside the 512-byte stack, offsets [-512, 0).
The 8-byte key slot is written, so the helper reads a defined key. Unprivileged programs may only read stack they wrote; since v6.3, CAP_PERFMON programs (all tracing) may read uninitialized stack.
The helper call is checked against its signature: r1 must be a map, r2 must point to key-sized initialized memory. After the call r1 to r5 become unreadable and r0 may be NULL.
The branch forks the state. On the taken path r0 == 0, so the verifier knows it is the scalar 0 and queues that path for later.
On the fall-through path r0 has been narrowed to a valid map value pointer, so the 8-byte atomic add at offset 0 is in bounds and allowed.
Both paths reach r0 = 0 and exit with a readable return value. Every path is safe, so the program is accepted and JIT-compiled.

blocks.prompt: Delete line 6 (the null check) and load the program again. What does the verifier do, and at which line?
blocks.reveal: It **rejects the program at line 8**. After the helper call, r0 has type map_value_or_null, and dereferencing it is an `invalid mem access 'map_value_or_null'`. The program never runs, so a missing key can never become a kernel NULL dereference. Deleting line 4 is subtler: an unprivileged program fails at line 5 with an `invalid indirect read from stack` error, but since v6.3 privileged tracing programs (CAP_PERFMON) may read uninitialized stack, so it loads and looks up a garbage key.

blocks.md: **Termination.** The verifier must finish its own analysis, and the program must finish too. Early verifiers rejected every loop (compilers had to unroll them). Since kernel v5.3, **bounded loops** are allowed when the verifier can prove the exit condition eventually holds, but it does so by walking the loop's iterations. Total work is capped: `BPF_COMPLEXITY_LIMIT_INSNS` is 1,000,000 *processed* instructions across all explored paths (before v5.2 the limits were 4,096 instructions and 128K complexity). So complexity grows with branches and loop iterations, not just program length.

blocks.title: Simplified model: verifier work for a loop

scenes.caption: Simplified model: processed instructions are roughly iterations x body size (real counts also depend on branches and state pruning). 100 iterations of a 20-instruction body is about 2,000.
With a 20-instruction body the 1,000,000 limit is reached at 50,000 iterations. Past that line the program is rejected even though it would terminate.
A 100-instruction body hits the limit at 10,000 iterations. Bigger bodies and more branches shrink how much looping you can afford.

blocks.md: When bpftrace reports that the BPF stack limit of 512 bytes is exceeded, its docs suggest using less data per probe (for example `pid` instead of the `comm` string), fewer map keys, or splitting the work across multiple probes.

The verifier runs once, at load time, and proves properties of **all** paths: bounded execution, typed pointers, null checks before dereference, initialized registers, in-bounds stack and map access. Because the proof is done up front, the JIT-compiled code needs no runtime checks and runs at native speed.

blocks.question: A program loops `for i in 0..N` where N is read from a map value with no upper bound check. The verifier rejects it. Why?
options: Maps cannot be read inside loops
Loops are never allowed in eBPF
The verifier cannot prove the loop terminates within its limits, because N could be any 64-bit value
The JIT does not support loop instructions
blocks.explain: Bounded loops are allowed (since v5.3) only if the verifier can show the exit condition is reached within its 1M processed-instruction budget. An unbounded N defeats that proof. Clamping N to a small constant first fixes it.

blocks.question: Which statement about the verifier is correct?
options: It checks programs at every execution, so bugs are caught at runtime
It only checks the first 4,096 instructions of a program
It lets tracing programs call any kernel function directly
It proves a program is safe for the kernel but does not judge whether the data it collects is sensitive
blocks.explain: Verification is a one-time load-time proof of safety, not a security policy. Access control is separate (root, or CAP_BPF plus CAP_PERFMON for tracing). Since v5.2 the complexity limit is 1M processed instructions, and programs call a fixed set of helpers rather than arbitrary functions.

lessons.title: Maps: counting, histograms and timing in the kernel

blocks.md:
Maps are what turn a stream of events into an answer. In bpftrace, `@name[key] = f(value)` names a map, picks its key (any expression or tuple, such as `comm` or `pid, comm`) and an **aggregation function** that decides how values combine:

- `count()`, `sum(x)`, `avg(x)`, `min(x)`, `max(x)`, `stats(x)`
- `hist(x)`: power-of-2 histogram; `lhist(x, min, max, step)`: linear histogram

Maps live for the lifetime of bpftrace, are shared by all probes, and are printed on exit. `$name` variables, by contrast, are scratch values on the 512-byte BPF stack that vanish when the action finishes.

**Why `count()` and not `@x++`?** Many CPUs fire the same probe at once. `count()` and `sum()` use **per-CPU maps**: each CPU owns a private slot, so updates are cheap and never collide. The price is paid on read, when bpftrace has to visit every CPU's slot and sum them. A plain `@x++` updates one shared value with no atomic instruction, so concurrent updates can be lost.

blocks.title: count() on 4 CPUs: private slots, summed on read

scenes.caption: The map value is really one slot per CPU. All start at zero.
Probes fire on all four CPUs at the same time. Each one increments only its own CPU's slot, so there is no contention and no lost update.
More events arrive: cpu0 has now seen 3, cpu1 2, cpu2 1, cpu3 4.
On exit (or a cast like (int64)@), bpftrace reads every CPU's slot and adds them: 3 + 2 + 1 + 4 = 10. Reads are the slow part, writes are the fast part.

blocks.title: Why @x++ can lose updates across CPUs

scenes.caption: Simplified timing: @x holds 5. CPU 0 loads it to add one.
Before CPU 0 stores, CPU 1 loads the same value 5. Neither CPU knows about the other.
Both store 6. Two events happened but @x only grew by one: an update was lost. count() avoids this with per-CPU slots.

blocks.md: **hist() buckets.** Latency and size distributions span many orders of magnitude, so `hist()` uses power-of-2 buckets. Value 0 and value 1 each get their own bucket, negative values go to one underflow bucket, and every value $n \ge 2$ lands in the bucket below. Finding the bucket only needs the position of the highest set bit, and the number of buckets is small and fixed, which keeps the per-event work tiny enough to do in the kernel. Labels use K = 1024 and M = 1024 x 1024.

blocks.caption: For example 905 has b = 9 and lands in [512, 1K); 1024 has b = 10 and lands in [1K, 2K).

blocks.md:
**Worked example.** One process does 18 reads with these durations in nanoseconds: 640, 710, 820, 905, 980, 1100, 1350, 1500, 1720, 2300, 48000, 52000, 61000, 70500, 88000, 97000, 131000, 250000. The first 10 are page cache hits; the last 8 had to wait for the disk.

The mean is about 45 microseconds (44,974 ns), a value that describes neither group. Below is what `hist()` prints.

scenes.caption: All values bucketed by their highest set bit. Two clusters appear: around 1 microsecond (cache hits) and 32K to 256K ns (disk).
The cached cluster: 10 reads in [512, 1K), [1K, 2K) and [2K, 4K).
The disk cluster: 8 reads from 32K up to 256K ns. The mean (44,974 ns) sits in [32K, 64K) and hides the fact that the distribution is bimodal.

blocks.md: **Timing between two probes.** To measure a duration you need a start time from the entry probe and an end time from the return probe. The standard pattern stores the start in a map keyed by **thread id**: a thread can only be inside one `vfs_read` call at a time, so `tid` uniquely identifies the in-flight call.

blocks.title: The @start[tid] pattern, step by step

scenes.caption: Thread 4211 enters vfs_read. The entry probe stores the timestamp under its tid.
Thread 4211 returns. The filter checks that a start time exists for this tid, so the action runs.
Duration = 5,000,905 - 5,000,000 = 905 ns, added to the histogram under this process name in bucket [512, 1K).
The start entry is deleted. Without this the map keeps growing, and stale entries could be reused by the next call.
Thread 4300 was already inside vfs_read when tracing began, so only its return fires. No start exists, the filter is false, and a bogus now-minus-zero duration is avoided.

blocks.question: A read takes exactly 1,024 ns. In which hist() bucket does it appear?
blocks.explain: 1024 = 2^10, so b = 10 and the bucket is [2^10, 2^11) = [1K, 2K). Bucket intervals include their lower bound and exclude their upper bound; only 0 and 1 get single-value buckets.

blocks.question: You remove the /has_key(@start, tid)/ filter from the timing script. What do you most likely see?
options: Nothing changes
The verifier rejects the script
A few enormous durations near the system uptime, from calls that started before tracing began and read a start time of 0
Every duration becomes 0
blocks.explain: Calls already in flight at attach time only hit the return probe. Their @start[tid] reads as 0, so nsecs - 0 equals the time since boot, which pollutes the top buckets of the histogram.

blocks.question: Many CPUs increment the same counter. Why does bpftrace recommend @c = count() over @c++?
options: count() uses per-CPU slots, so concurrent updates never collide; @c++ is a non-atomic shared update that can lose increments
@c++ is rejected by the verifier
count() is faster to read than @c++
@c++ sends an event to user space each time
blocks.explain: Per-CPU maps make writes cheap and exact. The trade is that reading the value is slower, since every CPU's slot must be summed.

lessons.title: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production

blocks.md:
eBPF tracing is low overhead, not zero overhead. A useful mental model: every probe hit costs some fixed time $c$ on the CPU where it fires (trap or trampoline, your program, map updates). If a probe fires $r$ times per second on one CPU, the share of that CPU spent tracing is $r \times c$.

For scale, the kernel's kprobes documentation measured 0.5 to 1.0 microseconds per kprobe hit on 2005-era CPUs, with return probes taking 50 to 75% longer. Modern CPUs, jump-optimized kprobes and fentry trampolines are cheaper, so measure on your own hardware; the model is what matters.

blocks.caption: 200,000 hits per second at 0.5 microseconds each consumes 10% of a CPU.

blocks.title: Tracing cost model: event rate times cost per event

scenes.caption: Simplified model at 1 microsecond per hit: 10,000 hits/s costs 1% of a CPU, 100,000 hits/s costs 10%, and 1,000,000 hits/s would consume the whole CPU.
At 0.5 microseconds per hit, 200,000 hits/s is 10%. Halving the per-hit cost (cheaper probe type, smaller action) doubles the rate you can afford.
Sampling at 99 Hz is about 99 hits per second per CPU: far below 1% even at 2 microseconds each. Rate, not probe count, decides cost.

blocks.prompt: Which costs more: a kprobe on a function called 50 times per second, with a fairly heavy action that walks a stack, or a cheap count() on raw_syscalls:sys_enter on a server doing 500,000 syscalls per second per CPU?
blocks.reveal: The syscall counter, by far. Even a heavy action at 50 hits per second is negligible, but 500,000 hits per second at, say, 0.2 microseconds each is 10% of every CPU. **Event frequency dominates.** Before tracing a hot path, estimate its rate first, for example with a short `count()` run over a few seconds or with perf's counters.

scenes.caption: Computed with rate x cost from the model above (assumed costs, simplified). Sampling and rare events are effectively free.

blocks.md:
**Practical rules that follow from the mechanism:**

1. **Aggregate in maps** (`count`, `hist`, `stats`) instead of `printf` per event. Output from `printf` is formatted asynchronously in user space; if bpftrace cannot drain its ring buffer fast enough, events are dropped (the buffer size is the `perf_rb_pages` config).
2. **Filter early.** A predicate like `/pid == 1234/` ends the program before map work.
3. **Prefer tracepoints**, then fentry/fexit, then kprobes, for stability. Expect kprobe scripts to break when kernel functions are renamed or change their arguments.
4. **Bound your maps.** Undeclared maps default to `max_map_keys` = 4096 entries; once full, new keys are lost. Keys like `kstack` or per-page addresses can need more.
5. **Sample** CPU questions with `profile:hz:99` rather than probing every function; 99 instead of 100 avoids running in lockstep with periodic activity.

Common misconception: "eBPF is safe, so tracing can't hurt production." The verifier guarantees the kernel won't crash or hang, but it does not bound *how often* your program runs. A kprobe on a function called millions of times per second can still cost a large fraction of every CPU.

Estimate cost as event rate x cost per event. Keep the rate low (stable, specific probes; filters; sampling) and keep the work in the kernel (maps, not printf). That is what makes bpftrace usable on a live production system.

blocks.question: You need to know where CPU time goes in a busy service, across all functions, for 30 seconds in production. Which approach fits best?
options: kprobe on every kernel function with kprobe:* and count()
profile:hz:99 { @[kstack] = count(); } and render the result as a flame graph
printf the stack on every sched_switch
uprobe on every function in the binary
blocks.explain: Sampling at 99 Hz costs about 99 probe hits per CPU per second regardless of how busy the service is, and kstack keys give a frequency count of stacks for a flame graph. Probing every function makes the cost scale with the call rate, which can be enormous.

blocks.question: A bpftrace script printing one line per network packet starts reporting lost events under load. What is the best fix?
options: Replace printf with a map aggregation such as @[comm] = count() or hist(), so per-event data stays in the kernel
Increase max_strlen
Switch the probe from tracepoint to kprobe
Run two copies of the script
blocks.explain: Lost events mean user space cannot drain the ring buffer fast enough. Raising perf_rb_pages only buys headroom; aggregating in a map removes the per-event traffic entirely.

blocks.question: A colleague's kprobe-based script worked last year but now fails to attach after a kernel upgrade. What is the most likely cause?
options: The verifier became stricter about printf
bpftrace no longer supports kprobes
Tracepoints replaced all kprobes
The probed kernel function was renamed, removed or changed, because kprobes target internal, unstable functions
blocks.explain: kprobes can attach to almost any kernel function, but those functions are not an API. Tracepoints, or fentry with BTF types, are more resilient. By default bpftrace exits with an error if any probe fails to attach, unless the missing_probes config is set to warn or ignore.
